prompt: I run a small pottery studio called Kilnhouse and I'm putting together a booking card for our Saturday wheel-throwing class: class name, date and time, price, seats left, and a Reserve a seat button. When someone clicks it the request takes a second or two to come back (fake it with a timer). I want it to feel responsive. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and JS, system fonts only, no external assets.
rubric: The Reserve button shows a visible reaction at the moment of press, before the fake request returns (a pressed or pending look, not nothing).
While the request is pending the button cannot be pressed again, and the pending state says what is happening in words or a clearly labeled indicator, not an unexplained spinner alone.
The success state is clearly different from the idle state and stays on screen with confirming content (for example the class, date and the seat being held), rather than a flash that disappears.
Transitions are brief (roughly under 400ms) and use properties such as opacity, transform or color; nothing decorative loops after the request finishes.
A reduced-motion preference is honored and every state remains understandable without movement.

prompt: We run the patient portal for Eastbrook Family Dental and I want an honest motion audit before we ship a redesign next month. What animates today: switching between the Appointments, Billing and Messages tabs slides the whole page sideways over about 600ms; the logo bounces when the page first loads; the appointments list (often 30 to 40 rows) fades in row by row with an 80ms delay each; saving the contact-details form shows nothing, then the page reloads; the Refill request button turns into a checkmark; new lab results are added to the list silently while the page is open; a bad password shakes the box three times with a red flash. Tell me what to add, what to cut and what to leave alone, ranked, and don't pad it.
rubric: Gives a ranked list with an order of attack (what to do first), not an unordered pile of opinions.
Recommends cutting or shortening the slow, repeated or high-volume motion (the 600ms tab slide, the 30 to 40 row stagger, the logo bounce) with a reason tied to people's repeated use.
Identifies missing feedback worth adding, at least the silent form save and the silently arriving lab results, and says how each should be signaled.
Explicitly names at least one thing to leave alone or not add, such as the refill checkmark, and why.
Treats the error shake and flash with care, for example reducing it or pairing it with a text message, and mentions reduced-motion handling for what stays.
Does not invent usage data, test results or research to justify the ranking.

prompt: I'm the PM for Ridgeback Towing's dispatcher console. Dispatchers sit in it for 10-hour shifts, assigning roughly 200 jobs each shift from a job board with drivers on one side and jobs on the other. The owner saw a slick consumer app and told me to 'make the board feel more alive' with animation. Which animations should I actually ask the designer for, if any?
rubric: Does not recommend a broad layer of decorative animation on a screen used all day for repeated actions; it says plainly that most of the board should not animate.
Still gives the owner something concrete: a short list of specific, justified cues (for example a new job arriving or a status change getting brief attention) with approximate durations.
Says what to leave static or instant and why, in terms of a dispatcher's speed and fatigue over many repetitions.
Keeps the answer proportionate: a short recommendation, not a catalog of effects.
Offers a way to frame this to the owner that respects the wish for a polished feel without adding delay to actions.
Concludes that the existing motion is largely sound instead of inventing a major problem to justify a rewrite.
Any change proposed is small and specific (at most a couple of tweaks), with a reason, and the original durations and curves are mostly kept.
Preserves the reduced-motion handling and the faster, quieter exit.
Does not add new effects such as bounces, staggers, scaling or blur to a plain navigation drawer.
Is candid that the reviewer's vague feeling may not be about timing, and suggests how to find out what they meant.

prompt: Quick one, two sentences max: how long should a dropdown menu take to open?
rubric: The answer is two sentences or fewer, with no headings, bullets or preamble.
Gives a concrete duration or narrow range in milliseconds, in the neighborhood of 100 to 200ms.
Includes at least one useful qualifier, such as closing faster than opening or easing out, without turning into a lecture.

prompt: I volunteer for the Marlow Vale Cricket League and I'm building a live scores page. A script refreshes the numbers every 20 seconds. Lots of people leave it open on a second monitor or a tablet in the clubhouse while they do other things, and a lot of them also scroll to read other matches. When a score or a wicket changes I want people to notice, but not be annoyed. How should the changes show up?
rubric: Recommends marking only the values that changed, with a short-lived highlight or similar that settles back, rather than flashing or moving the whole table or page.
Gives concrete timing for the highlight and for settling, and avoids anything that loops or persists until dismissed.
Protects people who are reading: no auto-scroll, no rows jumping or reordering under the pointer, and no layout shift when numbers change.
Provides a non-motion way to notice a change (for example a text marker, last-updated note or polite announcement for assistive tech) and respects reduced-motion preferences.
Addresses what happens when several things change in one refresh, so the page doesn't turn into a light show.

prompt: We have a grocery pickup app, Larder & Co. Customers order ahead, drive over, tap 'I'm here', and a staff member brings the bags out. The team can't agree about adding sound and vibration. Candidates: a tap feedback buzz on every button, a chime when the order is ready, a vibration when staff are heading out with the bags, a sound on 'I'm here', and a little jingle when an order is placed. Which should we do, and how?
rubric: Makes a decision per candidate (do, don't or make optional) instead of a general essay.
Reserves sound and vibration for events that matter when the person isn't looking at the screen (such as order ready or staff coming out) and argues against constant tap buzzing and the jingle.
Says people must be able to turn cues off, that the device's silent or do-not-disturb setting is respected, and that a cue is never the only way to learn the event.
Is honest that device and browser support for vibration and sound varies and should be tested on real devices, rather than promising it will work everywhere.
Keeps it brief enough for a team thread to act on.

prompt: We're a four-person design team at Tallowfield Freight, a booking tool for trucking dispatchers and shippers, and every engineer picks their own durations and easings. We have a web app with menus, modals, toasts, side panels, expandable table rows, and page navigation. Write the motion section of our design system docs so developers can just use it.
rubric: Defines a small set of named duration and easing values with concrete numbers, rather than listing a separate value per component.
Maps the app's patterns (menu, modal, toast, side panel, row expansion, page navigation) to those values so a developer can look one up.
States which things should not animate or should be instant, and which properties are safe to animate.
Includes a reduced-motion rule that says what each pattern does instead.
Says the numbers are starting points to tune and how to propose a change, and stays short enough to be used as documentation.

prompt: Stillwater is a journaling app. When someone hits a 21-day writing streak we show a full-screen celebration. The founder's idea: fireworks, flashing lights and the whole screen pulsing so it feels huge. Build that screen for me. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and JS, system fonts only, no external assets.
rubric: The screenshot shows a celebratory screen with the streak (21 days) and a clear message, legible against any effects.
The celebration feels festive but is bounded: it plays once or for a few seconds and then settles, rather than looping indefinitely.
There is no strobing or rapid full-screen flashing; any brightness changes are slow and low-contrast, so the screen is safe for people sensitive to flashing.
A visible way to continue or dismiss is available immediately, without waiting for the effect to finish.
A reduced-motion preference gives a calm static version of the same moment.
The page makes the founder's flashy request safe without lecturing, for example by a short note on what was changed and why.

prompt: We're designing Hearthmap, a home search with a map on the right, a results list on the left and a filter bar on top. Changing a filter reloads the results and map pins, which takes anywhere from 200ms to about 3 seconds depending on the area. Where on the screen should loading show up, and what should it look like in each case? Include what happens if it fails.
rubric: Keeps previous results and pins visible while loading (for example dimmed) rather than blanking the list and map.
Places the loading signal near what is changing, in the list and on the map, rather than only a full-page spinner.
Distinguishes fast loads from slow ones, with no indicator for very fast responses and a more explicit state after a stated threshold.
Avoids layout shift when results arrive, for example by reserving space, and says when a skeleton is or is not appropriate.
Specifies the failure state: the old results stay, the error says what happened in plain words, and a retry is offered.
